prompt.context: Our client is a major global oil company that owns the whole value chain: oil rigs, refining, distribution, and retail. Our direct contact is the CEO of the global retail operation. His operation consists of 1) gas sold at the pumps and 2) the convenience stores at the gas station. Profitability of the retail operation has declined, and the CEO would like us to help figure out why and to come up with a plan for the next five years.
prompt.question: Profitability of the retail operation has declined. Help the CEO understand why, and develop a plan for the next five years.

clarifying_info.q: What geographies does the retail operation cover?
clarifying_info.a: Global — the case will reference the UK specifically for benchmarking.

clarifying_info.q: What is the primary metric the client cares about?
clarifying_info.a: Return on Invested Capital (ROIC), defined as operating profit divided by invested capital.
Traditional gas stations and, increasingly, supermarkets that have opened gas stations in their parking lots.

framework: Diagnose the decline in retail profitability: split into gas/pump revenue vs. convenience store revenue
Assess competitive dynamics: understand the supermarket entrant's business model and market share trajectory
Benchmark ROIC: compare supermarket gas station vs. client gas station on fuel margin, convenience store profit, overhead, and capital cost
Identify levers the client can actually control (price, location, convenience store offering)
Recommend a focused improvement plan and pilot

questions.prompt: Over the past fifteen years, the number of gas stations worldwide has declined by six percent. What might be the causes of this?
questions.guidance: A strong answer identifies multiple distinct drivers: industry consolidation (fewer owners, fewer stations), higher dollar volume per station (fewer stations needed to serve same demand), changing population patterns (fewer rural stations as population urbanizes), and operational changes such as more 24-hour stations reducing the total number needed.

questions.prompt: Calculate the ROIC for the UK supermarket gas station. Numbers: sells 10 million litres/year at 72 cents/litre; cost 20 cents/litre; tax 45 cents/litre; convenience store operating profit 500,000 pounds/year; overhead = 10% of fuel sales; capital cost = 2 million pounds.
questions.guidance: Work through fuel margin, then add convenience store profit, subtract overhead, divide by capital. Candidate should note the convenience store is responsible for essentially all the profit — fuel margin net of overhead is roughly zero.

math.setup: Fuel revenue = 10M litres x 0.72 = 7.2M. Fuel cost = 10M x 0.20 = 2.0M. Fuel tax = 10M x 0.45 = 4.5M. Fuel gross profit = 7.2M - 2.0M - 4.5M = 0.7M. Overhead = 10% x 7.2M = 0.72M. Fuel net = 0.7M - 0.72M = -0.02M (approx 0). Convenience store OP = 0.5M. Total operating profit = -0.02M + 0.5M = ~0.48M. ROIC = 0.48M / 2.0M = 24%.
steps: Fuel gross margin per litre = 0.72 - 0.20 - 0.45 = 0.07 pounds/litre
Total fuel gross profit = 10M x 0.07 = 700,000 pounds
math.answer: ~24% ROIC; the convenience store generates essentially all the profit — fuel barely breaks even after overhead.

questions.prompt: Without running the numbers, what do you think the client gas station's ROIC will be, and why?
questions.guidance: Much lower than 24%. Key insight: same fuel margin and similar convenience store profit (only 20% lower), but capital cost is double (4M vs 2M) because the client's station is downtown. A downtown location commands a higher real estate premium, driving up invested capital and crushing ROIC.

questions.prompt: What causes the high cost of capital at the client's gas station?
questions.guidance: Downtown location — supermarkets are typically in the suburbs where land is cheaper. The capital premium of an urban location is the primary driver of the ROIC gap.

questions.prompt: Given the ROIC analysis, what levers could the client use to improve ROIC?
questions.guidance: Likely cannot change cost per litre (commodity) or tax (regulatory). Options: lower pump price to drive higher volume; relocate out of city centers to reduce capital costs; focus on growing convenience store profitability since that is where the margin lives.

questions.prompt: The client decides to focus on the convenience store and will pilot new products in 1,000 stores. What new products should be introduced? List at least eight factors that would guide the product selection decision.
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate a structured set of criteria. Strong answers organize by customer demand, economics, and operational feasibility. See brainstorming section for full list.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors would you use to decide which new products to introduce into the convenience stores?

categories.name: Customer demand
ideas: What does the existing customer want / what unmet needs exist at the pump
What products are needed frequently and will drive repeat visits
What products are durable (low spoilage risk)

categories.name: Economics
ideas: What products can be linked to existing high-selling items (basket-building)

categories.name: Operational feasibility
ideas: What can the company and its suppliers support logistically
What products can be sourced from existing supplier relationships
What products require little shelf space (space is at a premium in small convenience stores)

categories.name: Decision example
ideas: Hot and cold food was ultimately chosen: high margin, low shelf space, high visit frequency — though low durability requires careful inventory management

recommendation: Focus on convenience store profitability as the primary growth lever — fuel margins are structurally thin after tax and overhead
Pilot new high-margin, space-efficient, high-frequency products (e.g., hot and cold food) in 1,000 stores before broader rollout
Evaluate relocating or avoiding new capital investment in premium downtown locations to reduce invested capital
risks: Low durability of food products increases spoilage and waste costs if demand forecasting is poor
Execution risk in scaling food operations across 1,000 stores (supply chain, food safety, staff training)
Supermarket competitors continue to expand (30% UK share, 60% France) — convenience store improvement may not be enough if supermarkets undercut on price
next_steps: Define pilot KPIs (ROIC improvement, convenience store revenue lift, customer satisfaction)
Identify and contract preferred food suppliers for the pilot
Assess portfolio of locations for potential relocation or divestment of high-capital downtown sites
Monitor supermarket gas station expansion and model scenarios for further share erosion
